title: Query test runs with explicit semantics
relevance: SQL lets you investigate CI and service evidence near its source, with clear relational contracts.

sections.title: Rows, filters, and groups
paragraphs: SELECT chooses expressions; FROM supplies relations; WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters groups; ORDER BY orders the final result. Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed.
COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(duration) counts non-NULL durations. AVG(duration) ignores NULL. SQL comparisons with NULL produce unknown; use IS NULL, not = NULL.
sections.code:
SELECT test_id, COUNT(*) AS runs,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failures
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY test_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY test_id;

sections.title: The browser database
paragraphs: The lab seeds fictional builds, test_cases, test_runs, failures, and defects in DuckDB-WASM. No server receives your SQL. You can inspect data with SELECT * FROM test_runs.

Use GROUP BY for counts by module, CASE for indicators, and HAVING for minimum sample size. A CTE gives an intermediate result a meaningful name. It improves readability but does not necessarily force materialization.

sections.title: Engineering boundaries and independent checks
paragraphs: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(duration) excludes NULL durations. AVG also ignores NULL, which can conceal missing execution data if the report does not include a missing count. Use CASE to make denominator policy explicit.

Ordering is a contract when comparing query output in a test. Without ORDER BY, a database may return equivalent rows in a different order. Test all-pass, all-fail and NULL-status cases with hand-computed expected rows. Relational models should use stable keys and constraints for builds, cases, runs and defects; a test display name is a useful label but a weak primary key when names can change.

mistake: COUNT(duration) can be smaller than COUNT(*) when duration is unknown.
takeaway: Make NULL behavior and denominators visible in every metric.

quiz.explanation: WHERE operates on input rows; HAVING filters grouped results.

title: Join failures to builds and defects
relevance: Defect correlation requires faithful event relationships. A bad join can fabricate a spike in product failures.

sections.title: Preserving evidence
paragraphs: INNER JOIN retains matching pairs only. LEFT JOIN retains every left row and fills absent right fields with NULL. RIGHT JOIN is the symmetric concept; it can usually be rewritten as a left join with reversed tables.

Filtering a right-hand column in WHERE after a left join can remove the unmatched rows and effectively behave like an inner join. Put the match restriction in ON when retaining all left rows is the goal.
sections.code:
SELECT tc.name, COUNT(tr.run_id) AS executions
FROM test_cases tc
LEFT JOIN test_runs tr ON tc.test_id = tr.test_id
GROUP BY tc.test_id, tc.name
ORDER BY tc.name;

sections.title: Correlation is not causal attribution
paragraphs: Join failures to defects using an explicit defect_id when available. A shared time window or module is weaker evidence; describe it as correlation. Multiple defects per failure need a linking table and deliberate counting of distinct failure IDs.

UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL preserves them. Do not use UNION as a bandage for an incorrect join. Indexes and query plans help diagnose performance, but measure scanned rows and join cardinalities before guessing.

sections.title: Engineering boundaries and independent checks
paragraphs: A LEFT JOIN retains every left-side record, but a WHERE predicate on a right-side column can remove unmatched rows and effectively turn the result into an inner join. Put matching conditions in ON when unmatched cases must remain visible, and explicitly decide how NULL evidence affects the report.

Use EXISTS for membership questions when joined detail rows would multiply results. UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL preserves them and is appropriate only when duplicate events should count. Test one-to-many failures, unmatched defects and duplicate related records. Explain expected row cardinality before running the query, then compare actual counts. A plausible report number is not enough if the join changed the unit of analysis.

mistake: COUNT(*) after a left join counts the preserved unmatched row; count a right-hand ID for actual matches.
takeaway: Choose a join by the evidence you must preserve.

title: Latest results, ranks, and failure streaks
objectives: Use window functions without collapsing rows
Find latest execution per test with a CTE
relevance: Latest-state dashboards and consecutive-failure alerts depend on per-test ordering, not global timestamps.

sections.title: Windows preserve rows
paragraphs: GROUP BY reduces multiple rows to a group. A window function annotates each row using its partition. ROW_NUMBER() gives a unique sequence within a partition; RANK() gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps.
Use PARTITION BY test_id for independent sequences. Order by build_id DESC and run_id DESC to break ties deterministically. Filter row number in an outer query or QUALIFY.

sections.title: Lag and failure streaks
paragraphs: LAG(status) reads the previous row within the ordered partition; LEAD reads the next. Three consecutive executions failing is not always three consecutive builds: retries can add rows and missing builds create gaps.

Define a build-level status policy first, then check the current and previous two statuses plus consecutive build identifiers. Production build IDs may not be sequential; join to a build calendar or explicit sequence.

sections.title: Engineering boundaries and independent checks
paragraphs: A latest-result query needs a deterministic tie break. ROW_NUMBER over partition by test_id order by build_id descending, run_id descending identifies one latest run; RANK can return several ties. LAG and LEAD preserve rows while accessing neighbors within the declared order.

Three failures in a row is different from three failures anywhere in history. Filter-free ordered windows must preserve intervening passes; filtering failures before LAG creates a false streak. Tests with F,P,F,F and F,F,F make the distinction visible. Inspect plans to understand scans, sorts and joins, and evaluate indexes for the actual filter/order workload rather than assuming an index always improves performance.

mistake: Ordering only by timestamp when timestamps tie makes the selected latest row unstable.
takeaway: Define the unit of sequence and provide a stable tie breaker.

exercise.prompt: Return test_id and status for each test’s latest result. Latest means highest build_id, then run_id. Sort by test_id.
exercise.explanation: Partition by test_id, assign descending row numbers, and select rn=1 in the outer query.
hints: Start with the invariant: use window functions without collapsing rows.

title: Subqueries, CASE, UNION, and query plans
objectives: Subqueries, CASE, UNION, and query plans
Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects subqueries, case, union, and query plans with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. Verify a regression query against hand-calculated expected output and test tie ordering.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: A correlated subquery references an outer row and can express existence without multiplying it. EXISTS asks whether at least one related row matches; a join returns all matching pairs. Choose based on the desired cardinality, then inspect the actual plan.

CASE models conditional expressions, UNION deduplicates result rows, and UNION ALL preserves events. Deduplication is not a repair for an incorrect join. Relational modeling separates stable test identity, builds, executions, and failure annotations.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Use EXPLAIN to inspect operators and EXPLAIN ANALYZE when it is safe to execute the query. Examine filters, estimated and actual rows, join cardinality, and scan cost. Index usefulness depends on the engine and workload; do not assume an OLTP B-tree rule applies unchanged to DuckDB analytical scans.
For consecutive build failures, first reduce retries to a documented build-level outcome. Then LAG and LEAD operate over the build sequence. Require adjacency rather than merely three failed rows.
sections.code:
SELECT tc.name FROM test_cases tc
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM test_runs tr
              WHERE tr.test_id=tc.test_id AND tr.status='failed')
ORDER BY tc.name;

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: An inner join drops unknown test metadata. A many-to-many join fabricates additional failure events. Selecting MAX(status) does not select the status associated with the latest timestamp.

Construct a fixture with duplicate metadata, missing builds, and multiple attempts. Compare row counts after every CTE. Query performance diagnoses should explain work performed, not just whether a query appears short.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Verify a regression query against hand-calculated expected output and test tie ordering. Include the actual SQL, schema, sample count, and plan in the CI report. Use separate correctness and performance gates so a fast wrong query cannot pass.
SQL interviews reward explicit NULL and cardinality reasoning. In an AI evaluation store, incorrect joins can produce an apparent model improvement by silently dropping difficult cases.

mistake: An inner join drops unknown test metadata. A many-to-many join fabricates additional failure events. Selecting MAX(status) does not select the status associated with the latest timestamp.
takeaway: Verify a regression query against hand-calculated expected output and test tie ordering.

module: SQL For Test And AI Engineering
title: Consecutive failures: preserve passes in the window
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects consecutive failures: preserve passes in the window with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. In the bundled nine-run fixture, checkout fails in all three builds and should be returned once.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: Three failures somewhere in history do not prove three consecutive failing builds. Order every outcome by build and run identity, including passes, then inspect neighbors. Filtering to failed rows before a window calculation removes the events that interrupt a streak.
Define how reruns within a build are handled before counting consecutive builds. A latest-run policy can select one outcome per test/build; the streak then operates over those selected outcomes.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: First rank reruns by run_id descending within test/build and select row one. On the remaining complete history, calculate LAG(status,1) and LAG(status,2) partitioned by test_id and ordered by build_id. Select rows where all three statuses are failed.

For strict adjacent build IDs, also compare the lagged build IDs to current minus one and two. If a test was not scheduled in an intervening build, decide whether that missing observation breaks the streak and record the rule.
sections.code:
WITH history AS (
 SELECT test_id,status,build_id,
 LAG(status,1) OVER(PARTITION BY test_id ORDER BY build_id) AS prev,
 LAG(status,2) OVER(PARTITION BY test_id ORDER BY build_id) AS prev2
 FROM test_runs
) SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM history h JOIN test_cases c USING(test_id)
WHERE h.status='failed' AND prev='failed' AND prev2='failed' ORDER BY c.name;

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A query counts F,P,F,F as a three-failure streak after removing P. Another treats builds 1,4,8 as consecutive merely because they are adjacent observed rows.

Use tiny histories to test uninterrupted failures, intervening passes, missing builds and duplicate reruns. Inspect ordering and partition keys when results appear plausible but disagree with the declared policy.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: In the bundled nine-run fixture, checkout fails in all three builds and should be returned once. Login has two failures followed by a pass, and search has one failure between passes.

SDETs should compare exact expected names and explain why each excluded test does not meet the rule. Keep this query as a regression detector, not a claim that all repeated failures have the same root cause.

takeaway: In the bundled nine-run fixture, checkout fails in all three builds and should be returned once.
